meeting_header: Date: 2026-03-04 | Time: 14:00 PDT | Duration: 57m | Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Martinez (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Oakmont Head of AI), Jon Ellis (Cloud Architect), Priya Rao (Security)
summary: Discovery focused on Dedicated capacity for Oakmont Bank's LLM serving. Key topics: reserved GPU sizing, burst/elasticity strategy, isolation and data residency, security compliance (SOC2/KMS/VPC), expected scaling profile and performance targets. Agreed to share pricing, benchmarks, and schedule a technical deep dive.
topics: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
transcript: [00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Avery, AE on the account, with Luis from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Maya Patel: Hi, thanks. I'm Maya, Head of AI at Oakmont. We're excited to chat, we've been evaluating options for a dedicated inference fleet for our customer-facing chat assistants.
[00:12] Jon Ellis: Jon here, Cloud Architect. We're particularly concerned about isolation and predictable throughput for peak banking hours.

[00:18] Luis Martinez: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: understand current infra, scale and SLOs, why dedicated, burst/overflow strategy, and security/compliance. Then we'll outline next steps. Sound good?
[00:25] Priya Rao: Yes. Also we'll need to cover SOC2 and key management — that's non-negotiable for us.
[00:30] Avery Chen: Absolutely. Maya, can you start with high-level use cases and volume?

[00:36] Maya Patel: Sure. Two main products: 1) customer-facing chat for account help and 2) internal risk analysis assistant. Chat is latency-sensitive, p95 target around 350-400ms for short responses, while internal workloads can be higher latency but have heavier context windows. Peak QPS during business hours is about 180 concurrent requests, average token length 60-120. We expect growth of 30% next year. We also have strict data residency — all inference for EMEA customers must stay in eu-west-1.
[00:58] Luis Martinez: Okay so mixed workload. Are you currently hosting models with any provider or self-hosting?

[01:02] Maya Patel: We prototyped in-house with a couple of open models on Kubernetes but ops cost and tail latency are painful. We've also tried hosted APIs for POC but cost and lack of isolation are issues.

[01:12] Jon Ellis: And because of banking regs, we need either dedicated hardware in a cloud region we control or a private deployment behind our VPC. We prefer Redwood Dedicated if it can give us reserved GPUs and VPC peering.

[01:22] Avery Chen: Understood. On Dedicated we offer reserved GPU pools with VPC peering and private networking. We can isolate customer compute and provide predictable throughput. For bursting we support reserved capacity plus burst credits to a shared overflow pool — wanted to check if that kind of policy would fit your needs?
[01:36] Priya Rao: Burst is fine as long as data doesn't leave our tenancy. How does overflow work?

[01:40] Luis Martinez: Good question. Our burst policy can be configured to still run within a dedicated tenancy — essentially extra nodes are spun up within the customer's reserved fleet if they have capacity-based burst enabled, or we can fallback to a compatible lower-cost hosted variant but only if customer allows that in policy. For Oakmont we'd suggest dedicated-only burst or pre-approved region-level overflow to ensure compliance.
[02:00] Maya Patel: That sounds promising. What about GPU types? We have cost and perf targets; we were looking at A10 vs A100 class depending on model size.

[02:05] Luis Martinez: We typically recommend A100 or H100 for large 70B+ models, and A10 or L4 for smaller 7B/13B variants. Also quantization and kernel selection in our runtime can give you performance improvements — we'll share a guide. For your latency target of ~350-400ms at p95 for chat, with batching and KV cache we can likely hit that with a mix of A10s for most routes, A100s reserved for heavy offline workloads.
[02:25] Jon Ellis: What's the typical autoscaling behavior? We want predictable capacity but auto-scale during known spikes like monthly statement days.

[02:30] Luis Martinez: Dedicated supports scheduled scaling (time-based), reactive autoscaling (based on queue/backlog and GPU utilization), and manual buffer policies. You can set guaranteed throughput tiers per model and a max burst limit. For regulated customers we recommend scheduled scaling + conservative reactive scaling with a warm pool to avoid cold-start latency.
[02:45] Priya Rao: Regarding encryption and keys — do you support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations? We need to ensure keys never leave our control.

[02:50] Avery Chen: Yes, Dedicated and Private both support BYOK via Cloud KMS or customer HSMs. We can document the flow; logs show key usage but the keys remain in your KMS. We'll attach our KMS integration doc.
[02:58] Maya Patel: Good. On telemetry and auditing — can we get per-request audit logs and token-level cost breakdowns for compliance and chargeback?

[03:05] Luis Martinez: Redwood Console provides tracing and per-route token cost/latency breakdowns. For Dedicated we can retain logs in your S3 or push to your SIEM with ingestion controls. We'll surface request IDs and model versions in logs for traceability.
[03:16] Jon Ellis: How does model version pinning and rollouts work? We want canary deploys and automatic rollback on quality regressions.

[03:20] Luis Martinez: Rollouts: you can do canary % traffic, A/B tests, and automatic rollback if evals show regressions. For Dedicated we recommend keeping a stable pinned model for production routes and staging with automated promotions.
[03:30] Maya Patel: One of our concerns is cost: reserved capacity is great but we need to justify it. How do you help customers size the fleet to avoid overprovisioning?

[03:36] Avery Chen: We run a sizing exercise: you share traffic traces and target SLOs, we simulate and recommend SKU mix and reserved commit. Optimize layer suggests batching/KV cache settings and quantization tradeoffs. We'll send the sizing worksheet after the call.
[03:47] Maya Patel: Perfect. Also, do you support in-region private deployments for EMEA and US separately? We need data residency isolation.
[03:52] Luis Martinez: Yes, Dedicated supports region-specific dedicated pools. For strict residency we can pin workloads to specific regions and set routing policies.
[03:58] Priya Rao: Any gaps around SOC2, ISO, penetration testing reports? We'll need evidence for our internal auditors.
[04:03] Avery Chen: We can share SOC2 Type II attestation, ISO docs, and our penetration test summary under an NDA. We'll include those in the security packet.
[04:09] Jon Ellis: For the POC, we'd like to run workloads against your Dedicated fleet with a 48-hour sample, measure p95 and throughput. Can you support a short benchmark trial?

[04:15] Luis Martinez: Yes — we can provision a temporary reserved pool or use a pilot SKU with controlled quota. We typically run a 48-72 hour benchmark with your trace to produce a report showing cost per 1M tokens and latency percentiles.
[04:26] Maya Patel: Awesome. A few nitty-gritty questions: Do you support SSO (SAML/Okta) for access to the Console? Role-based access controls?
[04:31] Luis Martinez: Yes, SSO with SAML/Okta, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC. You can lock down routes and give token scopes per team.
[04:36] Priya Rao: What about data retention for request/response logs? We have retention policies and need the ability to redact sensitive PII.

[04:42] Avery Chen: You can configure retention windows and automated redaction rules; for sensitive fields we recommend client-side redaction before sending and using our structured logging to only capture non-sensitive metadata.
[04:52] Maya Patel: If we set up dedicated capacity, what's the typical lead time to provision reserved GPUs in eu-west-1?

[04:57] Luis Martinez: Lead time varies by region and SKU — typically 2-6 weeks for reserved pools in popular regions. We can accelerate in many cases with partner capacity or cloud provider procurement. We'll include estimated timelines in the pricing doc.
[05:08] Jon Ellis: Pricing model: is it flat monthly for reserved + usage for burst? Any minimums?

[05:13] Avery Chen: We do monthly reserved commits for Dedicated (configurable tiers) plus a metered charge for burst and overage. Enterprise deals can include blended pricing and SLAs. We'll outline examples based on your projected utilization in the quote.
[05:22] Maya Patel: Do you offer an on-prem/private appliance if we end up needing air-gapped deployments?

[05:26] Luis Martinez: We offer Redwood Private which is a customer-managed control plane and on-prem options for air-gapped environments. For now, it sounds like Dedicated in-region should meet your needs, but Private is available for stricter mandates.
[05:36] Priya Rao: For the benchmark, can you guarantee that customer data won't be used for model tuning?
[05:41] Avery Chen: We have clear data usage policies: Dedicated and Private do not use customer data to train our models. We can include a contract clause to that effect in the agreement.
[05:49] Maya Patel: Okay, that's important. One last operational question: what observability do you provide for token-level cost and where do we see the breakdown?

[05:55] Luis Martinez: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns per route and model version; you can export CSVs and push metrics to your billing system. We'll give you a demo of the Console in the next session.
[06:03] Jon Ellis: Sounds good. Are there known limitations around long-context KV cache sizes we should know about? We run some sessions with 20k+ tokens.

[06:09] Luis Martinez: We support large context via streaming and segmented KV caches, but at extremely long contexts you may see higher memory pressure. For those flows we recommend using specialized routing to larger-memory instances and limiting active context length when possible. We'll include recommended configs.
[06:20] Maya Patel: Thanks — that helps. Seems like the main blockers for us are final pricing, lead time, and security docs.

[06:26] Avery Chen: Understood. To recap next steps: we'll send pricing & timelines, the benchmark template, security packet (SOC2, KMS guide), and propose a technical deep dive next week. Anything else to add?
[06:35] Priya Rao: Please also include sample contract language about data non-use and the SLA details.
[06:38] Avery Chen: Will do. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with links and attach the docs. Luis, can you set up the deep dive invite?
[06:45] Luis Martinez: Yep, I'll send calendar invite for 2026-03-11 and include runbook and benchmark checklist.
[06:49] Maya Patel: Great, thanks. Look forward to the materials.
[06:52] Jon Ellis: Thanks all. Bye.
[06:54] Meeting ended
